meetings.label: Meeting A — March 4, 2027

speakers.name: Dr. Anika Rao
speakers.background: Dr. Rao is a cognitive-affective neuroscientist with 11 years of experience designing longitudinal adolescent neuroimaging studies. She manages wearable-sensor pipelines, MRI acquisition protocols, motion-quality control, and multilevel analyses of functional connectivity. Her prior work has examined sleep restriction, circadian timing, and amygdala-prefrontal network dynamics in teenagers.
speakers.distinct_perspective: She treats the sleep intervention as an opportunity to test whether changes in sleep timing and duration are accompanied by reliable within-person changes in neural circuitry supporting affective control. She emphasizes measurement reliability, repeated-scan design, motion and developmental confounds, and sample-size planning driven by scan-to-scan variability rather than only behavioral outcomes.
speakers.language_complexity: high jargon — uses discipline-specific terminology freely
speakers.epistemic_stance: highly confident in their discipline's contribution

speakers.name: Dr. Mateo Alvarez
speakers.background: Dr. Alvarez is a developmental psychologist with 9 years of experience studying adolescent emotion regulation, daily stress, and sleep-related changes in mood. He has led school-linked longitudinal projects using validated questionnaires, ecological momentary assessment, daily diaries, and mixed-effects models. He coordinates participant-facing protocols and is attentive to burden, assent, and age-sensitive interpretation of self-report data.
speakers.distinct_perspective: He frames the central question in terms of adolescents' lived emotional functioning across developmental stages: whether later starts alter how young people notice, manage, and recover from emotion in daily life. He advocates combining brief, validated regulation measures with repeated diaries, while probing whether reports are interpretable, developmentally comparable, and practical enough for students to complete consistently.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language
speakers.epistemic_stance: defers to other experts outside their domain

speakers.name: Dr. Camille Brooks
speakers.background: Dr. Brooks is an education researcher with 14 years of experience evaluating districtwide policy pilots, including secondary-school scheduling reforms. Her work combines implementation research, administrative-data analysis, interviews, and stakeholder surveys, with particular attention to transportation constraints, school climate, attendance, course performance, and equity across student groups.
speakers.distinct_perspective: She views later start time as a district-level implementation change rather than a laboratory treatment. She focuses on whether the proposed schedule is operationally feasible given bus routing and staffing, whether adoption differs across schools and families, and whether the policy produces meaningful educational outcomes such as attendance, grades, and stakeholder acceptance alongside any individual-level health effects.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Camille Brooks
transcript.text: Hi, everyone—before we get into the measures, I missed the end of the last meeting. Could somebody give me the quick version of where we landed on the student protocol? And today I mainly want to keep the district-side indicators in view too, so routing, staffing, attendance, course performance, and whether families actually experience the schedule change the same way across schools.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mateo Alvarez
transcript.text: Very preliminary. We were leaning toward one brief, age-appropriate regulation questionnaire, plus short phone diaries, so we can see whether sleep changes show up in day-to-day, uh, recovery rather than just in a retrospective score. But we hadn't fixed the diary frequency yet. I wanted to check the burden from the last school study, especially for the younger students, before we lock that in.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Camille Brooks
transcript.text: Mm, especially the younger cohort.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Anika Rao
transcript.text: Mateo, I’m curious about that too. Do the daily reports give us a separable within-person signal beyond the questionnaire, especially for the younger students, or are we mostly buying burden? For the imaging piece, that day-level variability could be useful, but only if the items mean roughly the same thing across, um, ninth through twelfth grade.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mateo Alvarez
transcript.text: I think they can, but I don't want to assume that yet. In the last diary pilot, younger students showed bigger day-to-day swings, but they also missed more entries. So that could be development, prompt timing, or just response style. I need to pull the burden numbers. Anika, on your side, how many repeated observations would you need before you’d- when would you call that a within-person connectivity signal rather than noise?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Anika Rao
transcript.text: For a change score, I'd want at least two scans per student, pre and post, but I'd feel a lot better with three if we can manage it, because single-session connectivity reliability isn't great in adolescents. The actual N depends on scanner access and motion exclusions, so I need to check both before I put a number in this column. Camille, once a district says yes, how fixed are the implementation dates? Our scan windows can't drift by weeks.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Camille Brooks
transcript.text: They're rarely fixed when the district agrees. The board calendar may be set, but routing redesign, union provisions, and sometimes a staggered school rollout can push the actual first later bell back by weeks. So I wouldn't anchor the scan schedule until we've seen the transportation assumptions and candidate-school contracts. And if one school's post window slides while another's doesn't, we need to treat that as implementation variation, not just a nuisance.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Anika Rao
transcript.text: I’d rather define the windows around each school’s actual first later-bell date and record the implementation lag explicitly. But if the post scans are offset by several weeks across sites, can the districts give us the routing and, um, bell-time changes at the school level, not just the board-approved date?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Camille Brooks
transcript.text: At the school level, usually, but I’d want the operational record, not just the approved calendar. The actual first bell, bus pickup changes, route disruptions, and any staggered grades. I’m also a little worried about differential scan completion. If the school with the roughest transportation rollout has more missed post scans, how sensitive is your connectivity comparison- how sensitive is it to that uneven participation?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Anika Rao
transcript.text: It could bias it quite badly if completion is related to the rollout disruption and also to sleep or stress. I'd model the school-level implementation timing and use all the available repeated observations in a mixed-effects framework, but that doesn't fix systematically missing post scans. We'd need completion rates by school and probably some contingency slots. I also need to know if transport disruption itself is something we can measure, instead of treating it as background noise.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Camille Brooks
transcript.text: I think we can measure it directly. I’d want a school-by-week implementation log with planned and actual pickup shifts, late buses, route changes, and maybe a short student item on whether transportation changed their morning routine. The tricky part is that parent reaction may be to childcare or commute disruption rather than the later bell itself, so I’d keep a parent survey item that separates those. We saw that disconnect in the last scheduling evaluation.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mateo Alvarez
transcript.text: That student item could help us interpret the diaries too. If a younger student's morning routine gets less predictable because of the buses, a change in reported regulation may not be the later-start effect in the clean sense. It may be the rollout. Camille, have families said much in prior changes about tolerating repeated phone check-ins, or does that mostly become a student burden, a family burden issue?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Camille Brooks
transcript.text: Mostly, it becomes a student burden. But parent tolerance matters when the check-ins spill into the evenings or they have to troubleshoot phones. I’d keep the diary protocol really low-friction and ask parents separately about contact burden, because families with unstable transport or shared devices may experience the same prompts very differently.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Anika Rao
transcript.text: That shared-device issue matters for actigraphy too, actually. Device adherence can look like a sleep-timing effect if the watch comes off or gets swapped around. In our wearable pilot, reported bedtimes shifted earlier after the adjustment, but actigraphic midpoint barely moved. I don't know yet if that's weekend compensation, diary interpretation, or adherence, so I'd want a very short wear-compliance check, I mean a wear check, alongside the diaries.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mateo Alvarez
transcript.text: I’d put that check right next to the sleep items, not make it another diary task. And we should probably separate a missed prompt from a completed report saying the watch wasn’t worn. Otherwise, especially with the younger students, we’ll fold adherence into both the sleep and emotion story.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Camille Brooks
transcript.text: I’d want us to cross-tab those adherence flags by school and by transportation exposure, not just overall. If missed wear or prompts cluster in the schools with the messiest route changes, that’s an implementation inequity signal as much as a data-quality problem, and we shouldn’t quietly average it away.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mateo Alvarez
transcript.text: Yeah, that’s important.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Anika Rao
transcript.text: For the imaging analysis, I’d want those flags available at the scan level too, not just summarized by school, because a week of disrupted transport could affect both who arrives for the scan and their sleep immediately beforehand. We should probably record the actual days since the later bell started for every scan, rather than calling everything just, um, pre or post.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mateo Alvarez
transcript.text: And for the diaries, I’d want that same actual-days-since-start variable, not just a pre/post label. The first couple of weeks may be unusually chaotic, so I’m not sure a student’s emotion report then is comparable to, um, say week five. Maybe we need to preserve enough dates to model that settling period rather than average it out.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Anika Rao
transcript.text: Mm, that makes sense.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Camille Brooks
transcript.text: That settling period is probably substantively important on the district side too. Could we keep the first two weeks visible rather than just treat them as bad data, with attendance, late arrivals, and the parent transport items by week? If the routes stabilize quickly, great. If they don't, we'll know the student measures are sitting inside a genuinely different implementation context.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mateo Alvarez
transcript.text: Keeping those weeks visible is better than trying to call them unusable. For the diary side, we can look at completion and emotion reports separately by week since implementation, and not assume early missingness means the same thing as later missingness. I still need to check whether our last school study had enough younger-student data to support that without making the protocol- without making the protocol heavier.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Camille Brooks
transcript.text: I think that’s the right question, because if the younger students’ completion drops in weeks one and two, we need to know whether that’s protocol burden or whether those schools are still sorting buses. Could we keep the diary schedule fixed for now, but make the implementation log and the brief family contact item available so we can diagnose that before we- before deciding it’s a developmental pattern?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mateo Alvarez
transcript.text: That works for me as a provisional hold. I’d rather not decide frequency until I’ve checked the younger-group completion and the age coverage on the regulation measure. Then we can see whether a fixed schedule is actually, um, interpretable across grades, rather than just uniform on paper.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Camille Brooks
transcript.text: Let’s leave it there provisionally. I’d just add, before we approach districts, I need to verify the preliminary routing model and any fixed union or contractual constraints at the candidate schools. Otherwise we may be designing around a rollout pattern that- that simply can’t happen.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Anika Rao
transcript.text: Once that’s clearer, I can check scanner capacity and, uh, realistic motion attrition against the actual rollout windows.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Camille Brooks
transcript.text: Okay, I think we should stop there—the rest can wait until the next meeting, once we've got those checks. Thanks, everybody.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mateo Alvarez
transcript.text: Thanks, all. See you next time.

meetings.label: Meeting B — March 11, 2027

speakers.name: Dr. Maya Patel
speakers.background: A postdoctoral researcher with 6 years of human cognitive-neuroscience research experience, including doctoral work on emotional episodic memory. She designs behavioral paradigms using negative and neutral image encoding, recognition decisions, and confidence ratings, and has run multiple fMRI studies linking medial temporal lobe activity to subsequent memory and recognition performance. She is responsible for protecting the interpretability and feasibility of the participant task and imaging protocol.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Frames the project around psychological constructs and observable behavior: what participants attend to during encoding, whether emotional material changes recognition and confidence, and how hippocampal and amygdala signals relate to successful memory. She favors analyses that preserve a transparent connection between trial events, memory outcomes, and brain activation, while remaining receptive to model-based measures if they clarify rather than obscure the experimental question.
speakers.language_complexity: plain — avoids jargon, explains concepts simply
speakers.epistemic_stance: open to other perspectives, willing to revise

speakers.name: Dr. Elias Werner
speakers.background: A computational neuroscientist with 12 years of experience building and evaluating formal models of decision-making and learning. His work combines hierarchical Bayesian estimation, drift-diffusion modeling, simulation-based parameter recovery, posterior predictive checks, and cross-validated model comparison. He has collaborated on fMRI projects that use trial-wise latent variables, such as evidence accumulation and decision thresholds, as regressors in neural analyses.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Treats recognition and confidence responses as noisy outputs of latent decision processes rather than as direct measures of memory strength alone. He argues that behavioral effects and regional fMRI associations should be interpreted through identifiable model parameters, with model selection constrained by recovery simulations and out-of-sample performance. He is wary of relying only on condition averages or unmodeled confidence bins when a mechanistic account of the choices is available.
speakers.language_complexity: high jargon — uses discipline-specific terminology freely

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elias Werner
transcript.text: Morning—before we jump in, did anyone catch Maya up on where we landed last time? I mainly want us to look at the behavioral export and decide what’s actually defensible for the first-level model. I’m seeing people with basically matched recognition accuracy but very different—actually, very different use of the confidence scale, which makes raw confidence bins a little worrying.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Patel
transcript.text: A quick catch-up would help—I missed the last bit. I agree raw bins may be awkward, but I don't want us to lose the plain questions. Did negative versus neutral items that were later remembered, or remembered with high confidence, show different hippocampal and amygdala activity? Before we split too much—too finely, what do the usable trial counts look like after exclusions?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elias Werner
transcript.text: The export on screen is before the final QC, so I don't want to quote a usable N or cell counts yet. I need to check those against the run-level exclusions. But those accuracy-matched, confidence-divergent participants are exactly why I'd keep the later-memory question and fit a hierarchical drift-diffusion model alongside it. Otherwise high confidence may be response caution or, uh, scale use, not stronger mnemonic evidence.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Patel
transcript.text: I’m open to that alongside the standard later-memory model. I just want to know, when you put those trial-wise model values into fMRI, what would count as evidence that they tell us something beyond correct versus incorrect and the reported confidence, especially if they’re correlated with reaction time or confidence? The negative false alarms are a little, um, odd in this export too, so I’d rather not assume high confidence is one thing behaviorally.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elias Werner
transcript.text: A significant trial-wise regressor on its own wouldn’t be incremental evidence if it’s just another way of expressing RT or the confidence report. We should compare first-level models, the standard subsequent-memory plus confidence model versus that model with the latent decision variable added, and ask if it improves held-out predictive fit while we check the design-matrix correlations. But first, Maya, in this task, do you expect confidence to track mnemonic evidence closely enough that it’s even plausible to separate it from caution?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Patel
transcript.text: I think it’s plausible, but not close enough to assume it. For most people, high confidence probably reflects stronger evidence, but the scale-use differences—and those high-confidence negative false alarms—I’m losing the point. Caution or response style could be mixed in too. So I’d treat the model as a useful separation to test, while keeping the observed accuracy and confidence effects visible alongside it.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elias Werner
transcript.text: I’d keep those observed effects as descriptive targets, not have the latent model erase them. What I need to check now is whether the trial counts and confidence-scale occupancy actually identify separate valence effects in a hierarchical drift-diffusion model. Then parameter recovery, posterior predictive checks, and cross-validation can decide the variant, rather than- rather than us picking one from intuition.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Patel
transcript.text: Mm-hm. Before we let the hierarchical model drive the fMRI plan, I'd like the basic post-QC table. Negative and neutral, hits and misses, plus false alarms if we're modeling retrieval. If the cells are thin, I'd rather- I'd keep the imaging question centered on subsequent memory and not try to estimate every valence-by-confidence interaction.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elias Werner
transcript.text: That seems right. I’m not proposing a saturated valence-by-confidence retrieval model if those cells collapse after QC. The hierarchical DDM can pool information, but it can’t rescue- it can’t identify parameters the data don’t identify. Could you scroll to the participant-level confidence-frequency column for a second? I want to see whether the upper-scale clustering is widespread or just those few apparent outliers.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Patel
transcript.text: If it’s just a few people, I’d be cautious about building the main model around it.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elias Werner
transcript.text: Possibly, but even a few people are enough to make pooled confidence bins hard to interpret, so I wouldn't make the whole model hinge on them either. Could you read out the counts at the top end by participant, say the proportion using the highest category? If it's broadly skewed, we may need confidence as an auxiliary observation with participant-level response-style variation rather than a simple ordinal regressor, but—

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Patel
transcript.text: Let's look at that before we decide how to code confidence. And could we keep the raw proportion and the number of trials there? A participant with, say, three highest-category responses is different from somebody who puts half the task at the ceiling.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elias Werner
transcript.text: Exactly, we need the denominator and occupancy, not just the proportion. And if the ceiling users are concentrated in one valence or response outcome, that changes the modeling question quite a bit. We should also read those counts split by negative versus neutral and by hit versus false alarm, if the sheet has that.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Patel
transcript.text: For the imaging side, I'd want the encoding trials still labeled by later hit or miss, even if retrieval confidence gets modeled more flexibly. If negative false alarms are where the ceiling is, that's interesting behaviorally, but I don't want it to quietly redefine the main hippocampal subsequent-memory contrast, because...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elias Werner
transcript.text: No, agreed, the encoding GLM should keep the conventional negative-versus-neutral subsequent-memory contrast exactly as planned. The retrieval-side model is complementary. If that false-alarm ceiling pattern survives QC, it tells us confidence isn't a clean mnemonic-strength regressor. It doesn't mean we should fold it into the hippocampal contrast.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Patel
transcript.text: Okay, I think that's enough for today. Once we've got the post-QC counts in front of us, we can, we can pick this back up. Thanks, everyone.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elias Werner
transcript.text: All right, take care.
